title: Second Hand AI-barrassment
summary: The American midterm elections are turning AI into another team sport, complete with slogans, sponsors, and trash talk. Canada and Europe should refuse to participate in this game, and instead take a more pragmatic approach to AI.
articleHtml:
Disclaimer: The opinions expressed in my writings are my own and do not represent the organizations I am affiliated with. I do not use AI to draft, write, or edit my articles. I do use AI for research assistance, debate, occasional image generation, and final reviews.

My current job title is Senior Manager of Artificial Intelligence, Cloud, and Data in a technology consulting firm. Prior to this, I was the Head of Advanced Technologies and Artificial Intelligence at a European space and defence company, with a team spread across UK, Spain, and Portugal. Prior to that, I was Product Manager for a space company in Canada building AI products.

This is not a LinkedIn-style humblebrag. I just want you to understand that I may know just a little bit about what it’s like to work in, with, and for AI in both Canada and Europe, so you take me seriously when I say this: regardless of where you stand on the “AI debate”,

Artificial Intelligence is too important of a technology for us to let a bipolar American political system decide its future.

I don’t think there is much question anymore on the fact that AI is important — whether it’s as important as the internet, electricity, the wheel, language, or fire, remains to be seen. On the flip-side, it also has very real and, perhaps, unprecedented costs — and whether that’s human extinction or major economic upheaval also remains to be seen. This issue, then, must be debated logically, intelligently, and completely — not through political sound-bites, post-truths, twitter posts, or culture wars.

The American midterms are coming for AI

Trump has recently come out gung-ho on Artificial Intelligence… or Super Intelligence (I can’t believe this is a real thing). He calls fears of AI destroying humanity a “hoax”, and claims those who speak out against data-centers and big-tech are simply falling for Chinese propaganda. Democrats, on the other hand, are using an overtly anti data-center strategy to try and find votes in swing states. America is, therefore, turning a complex but important question into a test of which team you support.

I typically roll my eyes at most “both sides” arguments, but this time I’m going to make one. AI is incredibly necessary AND humanity deserves protection from its consequences. The build-out of AI, therefore, deserves nuance, not American jingoism.

Canada and Europe are uniquely vulnerable to American second-hand partisanship seeping into our political and cultural make-up — something Pierre Trudeau compared to “sleeping with an elephant”. The memories of the “COVID hoax” and “vaccine injuries” are only too fresh in my mind. There is a direct line, in my opinion, between Donald Trump’s nomination for the Republican party and Brexit — both campaigns were built on the same underlying principles, and both campaigns were immune to fact-checking. There is no reason to think that this time around, the American political parties will suddenly decide to be factual and pragmatic.

Canada and Europe must not allow the AI debate in our countries to become a political tug-of-war. As big, powerful, and influential as it may be, let’s remember, America is a country that has been unable to reasonably regulate guns — machines specifically designed to take lives — due to staunch partisanship. Can we really expect them to responsibly lead global AI alignment?

Use common sense

A data center is like a highway. It is neither inherently good nor bad. The questions around it should shape it: What will it provide? What will it consume? Who pays? Who benefits?

A few months ago, my cousin in England expressed that she is against data centers. When I asked her why, she listed the usual greatest-hits: water, electricity, pollution, and jobs. How much water does a data center use? No idea. How much CO2 is produced to power a server? Dunno. Eventually, she settled on “I just don’t want machines doing human things.” All of these are valid questions, I think, and arguments worth having, but significantly different from where the conversation is heading.

Europe had an EU AI Act in the works before it ever had a frontier model — a laughably European phenomenon. America, on the other extreme, has had AI models break out of isolation and hack other companies — something humans could go to jail for — without any real consequences for the labs. The best course of action is probably somewhere in between these extremes.

My ask

I am not an expert in all things AI, far from it, but I do have some ideas. Both Canada and Europe must build within limits where the benefits justify the risk. Sovereign AI capabilities are going to be important — most of all for national security — therefore we must focus on sovereign models running on local data centers that cannot be turned off whenever the Americans want. For critical systems — such as defence, infrastructure, healthcare — vendor agnosticity is a must. For every major data-centre proposal, publicly account how it will pay for its electricity usage, what benefits the community will receive, its real costs, contingency plans, and then decide based on cost-benefit analysis, not surveys.

My English cousin and I may still disagree, but we should not need an American election to dictate what we think.
